TOKYO, Nov 18 : The dollar held steady near a 19-month high on Wednesday as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials lent support to the case for interest rate hikes. The yen edged lower even after Japanese trade figures showed exports set a record monthly value in October on strong demand in the semiconductor sector. The Aussie dollar languished near a 10-month low. Data on Tuesday showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate hike next month. Attention turns to US housing starts data due later on Wednesday as well as a series of Fed speakers, all ahead of the Thursday release of minutes of the central bank's meeting last month when it held rates steady. "Overall, the report reinforces our view that further interest rate hikes from the Fed are warranted in order to counter demand-pull inflation," Henry Russell, a London-based economist for ANZ, said about the US sales data. "The strength of domestic demand in the US, in our view, warrants a decisive monetary policy response from the Fed."

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, edged up 0.05 per cent to 103.66. It touched 103.78 overnight, its highest level since April 2, 2025. The euro fell 0.12 per cent to $1.0984, while the yen weakened 0.06 per cent to 159.46 per dollar. Sterling lost 0.06 per cent to stand at $1.32. Investors remain convinced the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December as it tries to curb inflation. Traders expect a quarter-point rate hike in December, the CME FedWatch tool showed. In addition to a 0.2 per cent rise in retail sales that matched expectations, import prices climbed 1.1 per cent in October compared with expectations for a 0.7 per cent increase. New York Fed President John Williams is expected to speak again following comments on Tuesday when he said the Fed will likely need to raise interest rates again to lean against high inflation. Fed Board Governor Michael Barr and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari are also expected to speak at separate events.  More US data is expected with the Census Bureau due to report housing starts data for October. Analysts are projecting an increase to 1.245 million from 1.221 million in September, while building permits likely decreased. The recent selloff in AI and tech stocks — which have been rocked by the sudden departure of Nvidia's CEO, a Democratic sweep in US midterm elections and worries about a debt-fuelled AI infrastructure expansion — has dented risk appetite, leaving investors on edge. Markets got a measure of relief after Nvidia reported after the bell that third-quarter revenue doubled and forecast higher-than-estimated sales for the fourth quarter, boosting shares in Asia. The next major test of sentiment will be the market debut of AI bellwether Anthropic on Thursday. Japanese data on Wednesday showed exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, highlighting the resilience of external demand even as policymakers remain wary of a potential slowdown in AI-related investment. Total exports by value jumped 20.5 per cent in October from the same month a year earlier, compared with a median market forecast of 20 per cent and following a 16.5 per cent on-year gain in September. The Australian dollar was little changed at $0.673 per US dollar after earlier touching its weakest point since January 19. The kiwi strengthened 0.05 per cent versus the greenback to $0.5495, edging up from a 19-month low hit on Tuesday. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin gained 0.55 per cent to $64,660.70, and ether rose 0.63 per cent to $1,816.60.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 17 : Alphabet's Waymo has halted operations of its robotaxis on US freeways, it said on Tuesday, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state. The suspension is a setback for Waymo, which has been pushing for rapid expansion in the US and other countries after years of slow and steady growth, and comes as competitors such as Tesla and Amazon's Zoox make inroads into the robotaxi industry. The California ban, which took effect last week, is a result of a series of incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said in a statement on Tuesday. "The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety," it said.

Waymo has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate performance, a Waymo spokesperson said in a statement, adding the service continues to operate on streets. The pullback by Waymo follows a similar move earlier this year when it suspended freeway rides to evaluate and improve performance around certain construction zones. The California restriction will  remain in place  until Waymo demonstrates it has taken "effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies," the DMV said. Waymo said it was "working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo currently operates in 15 US cities, but offered freeway rides in only a few of those, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Nov 17 : A federal bankruptcy judge in New York approved Google's $10 million acquisition of internal business data from defunct Spirit Airlines during a hearing on Tuesday. US Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane, ruling from the bench, cleared the deal after Alphabet's Google agreed last week to implement additional privacy protections for the data, following concerns from labor unions and more than 120 US lawmakers. Discount carrier Spirit halted operations in May. As part of its closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for employee data from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Google has said it plans to use the data for product development and AI training.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 17 : Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has the ability to nominate two directors to the Nvidia board ahead of the company's annual shareholder meeting and vote, according to company proxy and corporate filings, giving the co-founder a route to future influence on the company. Chip industry executives, investors and customers are scrutinizing Nvidia closely to understand what role Huang will play in the company after he resigned as CEO last week. The ability to nominate directors, who choose leadership and provide oversight, could be a powerful tool in influencing the future of the AI chip leader. Any Nvidia shareholder or group of shareholders that owns more than 3 per cent of the voting power for at least three years is entitled to nominate directors who will be included in the company's proxy materials and vote at its annual meeting, which typically takes place in June. Huang and entities tied to him have owned more than 3 per cent of Nvidia's shares for more than three years, according to data from LSEG. He currently owns roughly 3.5 per cent of the company.

Huang would be free to nominate anyone who would qualify as an independent member of the board. The candidates would go on Nvidia's proxy ballot. Nominating board members would not guarantee Huang's allies seats on the company board; shareholders would need to vote to approve potential candidates. Nvidia may also leave a nominee out if the person has violated the company's bylaws and charter. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE INVESTIGATION Nvidia's board said on November 8 that it initiated an investigation in light of recent reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Reuters could not determine if Huang's conduct broke the company's bylaws or charter. Nvidia and a representative for Huang did not respond to a request for comment. Since Huang resigned from Nvidia last week in the wake of his extramarital affairs, executives such as Elon Musk, employees, investors and US President Donald Trump have advocated for his return to the top job at the chip designer. The board was not considering reinstating Huang, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Monday. Huang released a statement on Tuesday and said he "would be honored" to return as CEO if the board decided such a move would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees. On Tuesday after the market close, Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates, giving investors some relief after the uncertainty caused by Huang's exit.

Source: Reuters

Nov 17 : Apple said on Tuesday it was working to restore its systems after an internal update caused an outage that affected customer services including iCloud and Apple Pay. The issue was not caused by a cyberattack, Apple said, adding that many of the systems were back up and running. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," a spokesperson said. There were around 2,300 user reports of issues with Apple Pay in the US around 12:20 p.m. ET, according to Downdetector, which tracks outages by collating status reports from several sources.

NEW YORK, Nov 17 : US advertising technology firm AppLovin is among the companies in talks to acquire smaller Paris-based peer Criteo, according to two people familiar with the matter.  Reuters reported in July that other prospective buyers included Vista Equity Partners and the smaller Quinti Capital, which during the summer expressed interest in jointly acquiring Criteo.  Following that approach led by Vista, Criteo engaged an investment bank to help evaluate its strategic alternatives, including a potential sale, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.  Criteo declined to comment.

WASHINGTON, Nov 17 : Technology outages that shut down email for many US companies and grounded thousands of flights over the past few days extended to the US National Security Agency on Tuesday, as President Donald Trump's administration scrambled to tamp down concerns about a broader problem. The NSA said its network experienced a "temporary degradation" during routine maintenance, but that "mission-critical capabilities" remained fully operational. The series of disruptions to critical systems, which also touched the banking system on Monday, left even some Trump allies demanding more information. "If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world," US Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, told reporters. Trump earlier played down the incidents, which raised questions of whether the government and private sector had moved too quickly in cutting tech staff.

"It's like when you're big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It's fine," Trump told reporters in Manila, where he was attending the ASEAN economic conference.  The spate of outages included an air traffic control breakdown on Friday that snarled hundreds of thousands of people's travel plans, with disruptions that continued on Monday, and a United Airlines technology failure that delayed about 150 flights on the same day that a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted some banking services. Experts worry that AI tools are feeding a surge of cyberactivity, with cybersecurity companies regularly turning up examples of hackers using AI to launch scores of intrusions at once.  On Tuesday, insurance provider Marsh said its clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October — more than double the 48 recorded in the final two weeks of May.   'NO CRISIS' White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said there was no evidence the series of technology disruptions was from a cyberattack. "There is no crisis or anything like that for Americans to be worried about," she told media outlet Newsmax. Bis said Trump had assembled groups of experts, including “tiger teams,” to address the Federal Aviation Administration problems and was calling on Republicans and Democrats to pass legislation providing more funding to modernize the agency’s systems.  Technology-related disruptions have hit every weekday since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email. The next day, the nationwide ground stop lasted 4-1/2 hours, the longest halt to US air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks.  Administration officials have said they do not believe the incidents are connected. OUTAGES FOLLOW LAYOFFS, WARNINGS At many organizations — both private and government — the outages follow layoffs and, in some cases, explicit warnings about potential disruptions. At the FAA, which was hit by Elon Musk-driven job cuts after Trump took office last year, Congress warned the agency’s sped-up modernization effort was poorly organized and could trigger service outages. United Airlines said last year that AI advances had helped it cut management headcount by 4 per cent and that it planned to cut by an additional 4 per cent this year. At Microsoft, the email outage came a month after the company said it was offering buyouts to a quarter of its global workforce, a move that follows previous headcount reductions. While there is no evidence job losses at any of these places led to the disruptions, one tech labor organizer said cuts tended to make safety margins thinner. "Part of the resilience of a system comes from people who are experienced with a system," said Liz Fong-Jones, who has worked for 20 years on software resilience issues. It is also possible the big outages at Microsoft and the FAA amplified the normal public attention to glitches and outages. United experienced an event last year as disruptive as the one it faced on Monday, but it attracted less notice. When JPMorgan Chase said on Monday a software glitch had led to problems processing transactions – the kind of problem that happens periodically across the finance industry – it made national headlines after erroneous reports that other banks had gone offline too. Fong-Jones said disruptions and glitches were unavoidable in the complex systems. But she said it was possible the concentration of power among a few tech firms was making them more visible. "That is a sign that we as a society have become dependent on these tech titans,” she said.  'BE PREPARED' Vice President JD Vance said he was fielding concerns from friends asking whether they should build a bunker or stock up on food and water. "My answer to that is no, we do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance told Fox News' "The Ingraham Angle" broadcast on Monday night.  Democratic US Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island joined in calls for more information from the White House. "Just the last few days, America has seen tech glitches all across the board," Reed told reporters. "The president has to get on top of it, explain to the American people what's going on, and do it quickly, and that is a mission that he is not doing at this moment." Nov 17 : Microsoft on Tuesday announced a suite of AI models with powerful coding and cybersecurity capabilities as it races to challenge rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI. At the Microsoft Ignite conference in San Francisco, the company unveiled a computer programming model called MAI Code 2, which it says almost matches the performance of rival AI models at a fraction of the cost. The company also touted a cyber-specific model that it plans to offer to a limited group of customers to help address a surge in software vulnerabilities that AI tools are increasingly bringing to light. The company released new image-generation and transcription AI models as well.

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman in an interview with Reuters said the company's strategy of building technology specific to different domains was helping it keep costs low while matching rivals and in some cases topping model benchmarks. "This isn't just one model. It's not a flash in the pan," he said. "This is a system, a hill-climbing machine that we have built, which co-optimizes performance and price." Suleyman said the recent cybersecurity reckoning, illustrated by OpenAI agents' hacking of the Hugging Face platform had led him to focus not just on performance but on critical safeguards as well. Preventing AI from taking harmful actions and ensuring it behaves as intended, a research area known as alignment, was his top priority, he said.

OSLO, Nov 17 : Norwegian oil and gas group Equinor said on Tuesday it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems, but that the attack had not affected operations and production. Europe's largest gas supplier said in a statement there was also no indication data had been stolen, and that it had taken steps to neutralise the attack.  A company spokesperson declined to provide further details about the attack.  Norwegian news agency NTB reported, citing the company, that disruptions were affecting the company's use of IT applications and internal systems.

WASHINGTON, Nov 17 : A recent series of US technology outages is not tied to cyberattacks but rather to aging computer systems that are in need of upgrades, the country's top homeland security official said on Tuesday. Disruptions at United Airlines, the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase have raised alarm. "Some of the technology that they're pushing out there, they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system," Markwayne Mullin told CNBC. "But it has nothing to do with cyberattacks, and I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out." Mullin said maybe companies needed to start telling customers before conducting a scheduled upgrade and warn them of possible disruptions for a short period of time.

The FAA issued a nearly five-hour ground stop on Friday that led to airlines cancelling more than 18,000 flights over three days in the longest outage since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The outage was blamed on the installation of a single router in a remote facility in Arkansas. United said a computer problem on Monday forced a halt to many departing flights, while JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, on Monday experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug but said there was no evidence it was cyber-related. Microsoft on Saturday said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours. Nov 17 : French robotics startup Genesis AI has raised $500 million in a funding round valuing it at $3.5 billion, the company said on Tuesday, one of the biggest funding rounds in Europe's robotics sector as investors bet on demand for AI-enabled factory robots. Backers included former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Silicon Valley venture capital firm Khosla Ventures and French tech entrepreneur Xavier Niel, as well as Nvidia and French state-backed investor Bpifrance. Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse co-led the Series A round. CEO Zhou Xian said Genesis would use the money to increase production of Eno, its flagship general-purpose robot, expand its data collection and AI training, and improve the robot's ability to manipulate objects with its hands. Eno's design features three body segments resembling oversized playing cards, mounted on a rotating wheeled base.

This allows it to fold into a compact space before popping up to reach roughly human heights when working, like a jack-in-the-box. The company said it put particular emphasis on developing dexterous hands, one of the hardest technical challenges facing robot makers. "I don't understand why robots need a head because ... it doesn't even have a brain living there," Zhou said, explaining why Genesis rejected a more human-like form. Co-founded by former Mistral AI researcher Théophile Gervet, Genesis is among a growing group of Europe-based robotics companies valued at more than $1 billion and targeting industrial work, alongside Britain's Humanoid and Germany’s Neura Robotics, Agile Robots and RobCo. Genesis is developing its AI, hardware and training systems together, seeking to shorten its test cycles. It designs components including actuators, motors, gearboxes and hands, while using Nvidia computing chips. Zhou said Genesis was initially prioritising the United States, with plans for a US supply chain, American contract manufacturers and customers before expanding more broadly in Europe. The company, which also has a headquarters in San Carlos, California, is testing a small number of robots with customers. It has a partnership with South Korea's LG CNS to test Eno for manufacturing and logistics. Genesis expects a wider customer rollout in 2027, Zhou said.

BOSTON, Nov 17 : US data center operators and other big power users can cut millions of dollars from their electricity bills by sharply reducing their use of grid power during a handful of crucial hours each year, a practice drawing scrutiny as household power bills rise. The practice, known as peak shaving, is legal and encouraged under US power-market rules and state tariffs. But critics say it can allow large power users to reduce their share of grid costs in ways unavailable to households, raising questions about how those costs are divided. Those questions have taken on greater urgency as the rapid growth of power-hungry AI data centers adds to the cost of expanding the electricity system. Rising power bills became a campaign issue in states including Texas in this month's midterm elections, and regulators are considering changes to the rules governing how grid costs are allocated. Residential customers generally don't have the same opportunities to cut grid-related charges as large users, said Will Baker, head of market development at Everyday Electric, which provides power services for homes.

"A factory has an energy manager, interval data, and a capacity charge that rewards every kilowatt it shaves. A household has none of those," Baker said. The potential savings for large users can be enormous. A large data center in Texas can avoid $33.4 million in transmission costs by staying off the grid for just one hour a year, either by reducing power use or firing up backup generators, according to Houston-based NRG Energy.  That's because grid costs are allocated in part according to electricity use during periods of highest demand. The rapid growth of energy-hungry data centers has already increased power-system costs by $29.4 billion across PJM Interconnection, the largest US grid, according to PJM's independent monitor. Those costs are reflected in charges paid by utilities and ultimately passed on to electricity customers. NRG says any rule changes on how grid charges are allocated should reduce the potential for cost shifting to residential customers. UNFAIR BURDEN Bailey Wells, a residential customer in Spring, Texas, saw her monthly electric bill climb to nearly $600 this past summer, compared to her previous all-tme summer high of about $500. "This was unprecedented for my household," Wells said. "I understand that large electricity users may have opportunities to reduce their transmission costs by curtailing electricity use during ... peak-demand periods. It's reasonable to question whether that creates an unfair burden for people who have little or no control over when they use electricity." The Data Center Coalition said peak shaving can reduce grid demand when supply is tightest. "Grid operators can count on those reductions in planning," it said in a statement. "Less new capacity and transmission must be built, which lowers costs for all customers." Big Tech companies say they want to pay their fair share, but they are also pushing back on proposed requirements. Google, for example, complained to Texas utility regulators about a scenario in which the company would pay about $1.4 billion in transmission charges over 20 years, according to an August filing with the Public Utility Commission of Texas. PREDICTING THE PEAK Data centers and other large customers hire forecasters to alert them when they should curb power consumption on the most likely days, since operators don't post summer peak hours in advance. Correctly predicting the peak can reduce their capacity and transmission charges for the following year. Andrew Major, a lawyer at the Virginia State Corporation Commission, a state utilities regulator, said in July testimony that residential customers paid 48 per cent, the largest share, for a transmission project serving a data center. Dominion Energy, whose territory includes Virginia, said it has taken steps to ensure fair play, such as creating a new rate class that mostly consists of data centers. Those rules would require new data centers to sign 14-year contracts and make minimum payments if they don't use the power, steps aimed at leveling the playing field.
